https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: Troy School District's Middle School Curriculum Guide for 2024-2025 states the district's middle school philosophy, nine program goals, five graduate outcomes, and the complete course catalog for grades 6, 7 and 8. Sixth graders take five academic classes plus required every-other-day physical education, while seventh and eighth graders take four academic classes plus required half-year Health/Physical Education and Digital Applications 1.0. Algebra 1 Honors, Geometry Honors and World Language I are taken in eighth grade, each earning high school credit and counting toward the high school GPA. The 18-page guide also catalogs more than two dozen half-year and full-year electives in visual art, music, computer science, engineering, media and life skills.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
**Publication**
Troy School District Middle School Curriculum Guide, 2024-2025, 18 pages, presented to the Board of Education on February 11, 2025.

**Philosophy and Goals**
Troy middle schools provide a program that recognizes, accepts, respects and meets the diverse needs of young adolescents, characterized by a research-based curriculum with effective assessment and evaluation; a shared vision fostering respect for learning, diversity and responsible behavior; and a cooperative partnership with parents and community. Nine goals are listed, covering developmentally appropriate programs, meeting the needs of a diverse student population, core-subject skills and knowledge, discovery of special interests and aptitudes, diversified cultural/social/civic/vocational/recreational experiences, guidance services promoting self-esteem and responsible behavior, community partnerships, transition from elementary to high school, and modeling healthy lifestyles.

**Outcomes**
Five student outcomes: a self-directed learner, a quality worker, a positive communicator, a collaborative and cooperative contributor, and an involved and visionary citizen.

**Three-Year Overview**

| Grade | Academic load | Additional requirements |
|---|---|---|
| 6 | Five academic classes | Physical Education EOD required; music students may add Orchestra EOD, Choir EOD, Band EOD, Art EOD |
| 7 | Four academic classes | Health/Physical Education half year; Digital Applications 1.0 half year; music option of Concert Band, Chamber Orchestra or Choir full year; elective total of one full year |
| 8 | Four academic classes | Music option of Symphonic Band, Advanced Orchestra or Choir full year; elective total of one full year for music students, two full-year classes for non-music students |

EOD is defined as Every Other Day.

**Grade 6 Courses**
Required: ELA 6, Language Arts 6, Mathematics 6 (or another math class), Physical Education 6, Science 6, Social Studies 6. Mathematics 6 is organized into ten units: Area and Surface Area; Introducing Ratios; Linear Relationships; Unit Rates and Percentages; Dividing Fractions; Arithmetic in Base Ten; Expressions and Equations; Rational Numbers; Data Sets and Distributions; Putting it all Together. Grade 6 electives meet every other day alternating with PE: Art 6, Band 6 or Orchestra 6, and 6th Grade Choir.

**Grade 7 Courses**
Digital Applications 1.0 (half year, required), English 7, Health and Physical Education 7 (half year, a ten-week course covering nutrition, recognizing influences, human sexuality and choosing healthy behaviors, with parental excusal permitted), Mathematics 7, Science 7, and Social Studies 7, which surveys ancient world history and geography from the beginning until around 1500.

**Grade 8 Courses**
Algebra 1 Honors (five critical areas), English 8, Geometry Honors (six critical areas), Mathematics 8, Science 8, and United States History 8, which surveys U.S. history from the time of the Native Americans to 1877. Algebra 1 Honors and Geometry Honors count toward high school credit and the high school GPA.

**Electives**
Half-year electives for grades 7 and 8: 2D Visual Art, 3D Visual Art, Applied Engineering, Art Expressions, Ceramics, Communication Arts, Computer Programming, Computer Science Discoveries, Creation Lab, Digital Applications 2.0, Innovation Incubator, Life Skills, LINKS (teacher recommendation only), Money Matters, Science and Engineering Explorations, Theatre Arts, Video Technology, and Video Technology 2. Grade 7 full-year electives: Chamber Orchestra, Choir 7, 7th/8th Choir, Concert Band, Graphic Design/Yearbook. Grade 8 electives: 7th/8th Choir, Advanced Orchestra, Choir 8, Fundamentals of Fitness, Graphic Design/Yearbook, Jazz Band, Physical Education, Symphonic Band, WEB Leadership, and World Language I in Chinese I, French I, German I, Japanese I and Spanish I.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
The Troy School District Middle School Curriculum Guide for 2024-2025 is an 18-page publication appearing on the Board of Education agenda of February 11, 2025. It opens with the district's middle school philosophy: Troy middle schools provide a program that creates an environment recognizing, accepting, respecting and meeting the diverse needs and characteristics of young adolescent students, committed to academic excellence and to being developmentally responsive to adolescents' innate curiosity, desire to expand their environment, and need for recognition and personal achievement. The program is characterized by a research-based curriculum with effective assessment and evaluation that is challenging, integrative and exploratory; a shared vision with all members of the educational community fostering respect for learning, diversity and responsible behavior; and a cooperative partnership with parents and community members.

Nine Middle School Goals are enumerated. Goal 1: all programs will be developmentally appropriate. Goal 2: ensure all programs meet the needs of a diverse student population. Goal 3: ensure all students develop skills and knowledge in the core subject areas. Goal 4: provide opportunity to discover special interests, attitudes, aptitudes and abilities. Goal 5: provide diversified experiences in cultural, social, civic, vocational and recreational programs. Goal 6: provide guidance services and programs promoting self-esteem, independence and responsible behavior. Goal 7: provide opportunity to establish partnerships with the community. Goal 8: provide a transition from elementary to high school. Goal 9: provide a model for healthy lifestyles.

Five Middle School Outcomes follow: a self-directed learner who is responsible, enthusiastic, thinks independently and is open-minded and intellectually curious; a quality worker who designs a plan, applies resources, technologies and organizational strategies, creates products and performances, monitors development, maintains high standards and assesses results; a positive communicator; a collaborative and cooperative contributor who creates and sustains productive group relationships, respects the contributions of others, helps resolve conflicts and stays focused and task oriented; and an involved and visionary citizen who develops awareness of global issues, contributes to local and world communities, advocates for the environment and prepares to meet future challenges.

The three-year middle school overview specifies that all sixth graders take five academic classes; seventh and eighth graders each take four academic classes. Sixth grade requires Physical Education on an every-other-day (EOD) basis for both music and non-music students, with Orchestra EOD, Choir EOD, Band EOD and Art EOD listed as the alternating options. Seventh grade requires Health/Physical Education for a half year and Digital Applications 1.0 for a half year, plus, for music students, one of Concert Band (full year), Chamber Orchestra (full year) or Choir (full year); the elective load totals one full year, taken as two half-year classes or one full-year class. Eighth grade music students choose among Symphonic Band (full year), Advanced Orchestra (full year) and Choir (full year); non-music eighth graders carry an elective total of two full-year classes, taken as four half-year classes, two half-year classes plus one full-year class, or two full-year classes.

Grade 6 required courses are ELA 6 (full year), which studies literature of various genres and informational text including literary nonfiction with emphasis on inference from textual evidence, thematic and character development, claims and evidence, academic vocabulary and independent choice reading; Language Arts 6 (full year), covering narrative, informational and argumentative writing using mentor texts and the writing process; Mathematics 6 (full year, or another math class), covering ratio and rate, dividing fractions by fractions, negative numbers and variables; Physical Education 6 (full year EOD), run either as a yearlong every-other-day program or an everyday semester class; Science 6 (full year), with units on cells and heredity, ecology, Earth's changing surface, and species adaptation and survival; and Social Studies 6 (full year), a geography-based course covering physical and human geography, migration and settlement, culture and cultural diffusion, population and demographic changes, resource use, and trade and economic interdependence. Mathematics 6 lists ten units: Unit 1 Area and Surface Area; Unit 2 Introducing Ratios; Unit 3 Linear Relationships; Unit 4 Unit Rates and Percentages; Unit 5 Dividing Fractions; Unit 6 Arithmetic in Base Ten; Unit 7 Expressions and Equations; Unit 8 Rational Numbers; Unit 9 Data Sets and Distributions; Unit 10 Putting it all Together.

Grade 6 elective courses meet every other day, alternating with PE: Art 6 (full year EOD), Band 6 or Orchestra 6 (full year EOD, with fifth-grade band or orchestra or prior formal instruction expected), and 6th Grade Choir (full year EOD), which follows the National Core Arts Standards of Perform, Create, Respond and Connect.

Grade 7 required courses are Digital Applications 1.0 (half year), covering 21st Century and Web 2.0 online tools; English 7 (full year); Health and Physical Education 7 (half year), a combined ten-week course covering nutrition, recognizing influences, human sexuality and choosing healthy behaviors, with units countering messages encouraging tobacco, alcohol and other drug use and information on the spread of AIDS and sexually transmitted diseases, and with parents permitted to excuse their child from sessions on human sexuality and AIDS; Mathematics 7 (full year, or another math class), extending rates and ratios to proportional relationships and all rational numbers; Science 7 (full year), covering Earth's waters, weather and climate, astronomy, waves, energy, physical and chemical changes, and chemical properties; and Social Studies 7 (full year), focused on ancient world history and geography with content literacy, investigating human history from the beginning until around 1500.

Grade 8 courses are Algebra 1 Honors (full year, or another math class), a first-year high school algebra course for advanced students with five critical areas covering linear equations and inequalities, functions and sequences, regression techniques, exponential/quadratic/rational equations and systems, and specialized functions including absolute value, step and piecewise-defined; English 8 (full year); Geometry Honors (full year, or another math class) for advanced students who have completed Algebra 1 Honors, with six critical areas covering congruence and rigid motions, similarity and right triangle trigonometry, coordinate geometry, circles, geometric measurement in two and three dimensions, and geometric modeling; Mathematics 8 (full year, or another math class), covering linear relationships, linear equations in one and two variables, functions and irrational numbers; Science 8 (full year), covering energy, biogeochemical cycles, resources and human impacts, the rock cycle, Earth's interior, plate tectonics, earthquakes, volcanoes, hydrogeology, severe weather, Earth in space, the sun, Earth history and geologic time and climate change, including an online Moodle project; and United States History 8 (full year), surveying U.S. history from the time of the Native Americans to 1877, with detailed study of the American Revolution, formation of the national government, westward movement, and the Civil War and Reconstruction, and periodic study of Michigan history and U.S. foreign affairs. Both Algebra 1 Honors and Geometry Honors count toward high school credit and are figured into the high school GPA.

Half-year elective courses for grades 7 and 8 are 2D Visual Art; 3D Visual Art (papier-mache, clay, batik and mixed media); Applied Engineering (stress analysis, mechanical engineering, renewable energy systems, aerodynamics, space and rocketry); Art Expressions; Ceramics (pinch, coil and slab construction); Communication Arts (public speaking, pantomime, roleplaying, interviews, listening skills, improvisation); Computer Programming (Introduction to JavaScript: Drawing and Animation, JavaScript: Games and Visualizations, HTML/CSS: Making Webpages, HTML/JS: Making Webpages Interactive, plus building and programming a robot); Computer Science Discoveries; Creation Lab (bridge building, soldering, coding, game creation, projectiles, S.T.E.A.M. focus); Digital Applications 2.0 (Adobe Creative Suite, video production, animation, digital imaging, Dreamweaver; prerequisite is successful completion of Digital Applications 1.0); Innovation Incubator, whose cornerstone is the Larson Innovation Shark Tank project in which teams pitch inventions to members of the Metro Detroit business community including market researchers, patent attorneys and engineers; Life Skills (food preparation and hand and machine sewing); LINKS, a peer-to-peer support program pairing general education students with students with Autism Spectrum Disorder and other special needs, by teacher recommendation only; Money Matters (Michigan Career Pathways, budgets, bank accounts, credit, interest, investing and responsible spending); Science and Engineering Explorations, which prepares work for competitions such as the Science and Engineering Fair of Metro Detroit (SEFMD); Theatre Arts, which includes a public performance; Video Technology, using Windows Movie Maker and Apple iMovie with live morning news broadcasts and media literacy and copyright ethics; and Video Technology 2.

Grade 7 full-year electives are Chamber Orchestra, Choir 7, 7th/8th Choir, Concert Band, and Graphic Design/Yearbook, the latter connecting students with the Boulan Park School Community. Grade 8 electives are 7th/8th Choir, Advanced Orchestra (which requires many evening performances plus a Saturday performance at the MSBOA Orchestra Festival), Choir 8, Fundamentals of Fitness, Graphic Design/Yearbook, Jazz Band (by audition or teacher approval, with members also participating in a concert band ensemble), Physical Education, Symphonic Band (requiring many evening performances plus two Saturday performances including MSBOA Band Festival), WEB Leadership (Where Everyone Belongs, covering sixth grade orientation, school character and culture programs, charity opportunities and student mentoring), and World Language I. World Language I is a full-year, every-day course counting toward high school credit and the high school GPA, offered in Chinese I, French I, German I, Japanese I and Spanish I; the guide warns the class may only be offered at the high school during 1st hour, that parents would need to provide transportation to the high school, and that a shuttle will bring students back to the middle school.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: A Business Services Update presented at the Troy School District Board Retreat on March 8, 2025 walks through the 2025-26 budget schedule, the structure of school funding, the General Fund 2024-25 Amendment 2, and Amendment 1 for each ancillary fund. The presentation states that the district's 2024-25 foundation allowance of $10,394 is $4,236 per pupil less than the inflation-adjusted foundation allowance, a deficit equating to approximately $51.9 million in lower revenue for Troy School District that school year. Amendment 2 revenues are described as a 1.4% increase from Amendment 1, built on an audited FTE count of 12,272.

**Presentation**
Business Services Update, Board Retreat, March 8, 2025, attached to the March 18, 2025 agenda item 5.H.

**Budget Schedule**
April-May: develop 2025-26 budgets and 2024-25 final amendments. June: adoption and 2024-25 budget amendment (final, all funds), plus public hearing and millage rate adoption. June-October: audit of 24-25 financial statements and federal programs.

**Understanding School Funding (2024-25)**
The foundation allowance is built from state aid, a Non-Homestead Levy of $2,804 per pupil, and a Hold-Harmless Levy of $786 per pupil, with the amount dependent upon voter approval given as $3,590. Other revenue sources listed are sales, income, use, liquor and excise taxes, cigarette taxes and lottery proceeds.

**Foundation Allowance Breakdown**

| Year | State | Local (Non-Homestead) | Hold Harmless (Homestead) | Total |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2020-21 | $6,251 | $2,030 | $1,034 | $9,315 |
| 2021-22 | $6,523 | $2,121 | $786 | $9,430 |
| 2022-23 | $6,733 | $2,355 | $786 | $9,874 |
| 2023-24 | $6,971 | $2,637 | $786 | $10,394 |
| 2024-25 | $6,804 | $2,804 | $786 | $10,394 |

The presentation states the $4,236 per pupil foundation allowance deficit equates to approximately $51.9 million in lower revenue for the district this school year.

**General Fund Amendment 2**
Revenue adjustments, a 1.4% increase from Amendment 1, rest on audited FTE of 12,272 and a foundation of $10,394, with state-source items for 31aa Mental ($1.1m) and 147g 3% Reimburse ($1.6m); federal items for Title Carryover ($250k), Water First ($55k) and Effective Tech ($20k); further state items for Prior Year Adjustment ($600k) and 32n Out of School ($240k); and a transfer for the GASB 87 entry ($525k). Expenditure adjustments are described as a 1.9% decrease from Amendment 2: salaries and benefits adjusted for current staffing and lane adjustments plus new Schedule C items, grants updated for carryover and final allocations, and debt service/capital outlay for GASB 87 leases ($525k).

**Ancillary Funds**
Food Service Fund, Community Service Fund (fee-for-service programs including CARE company and community recreation), Troy Preschool Fund, TCC Grant Fund (Michigan Works! Troy), and Sinking Fund, each on Amendment 1.

**Food Service Fund**

| Line | 2023-24 Actual | 2024-25 Original Budget | 2024-25 Recommended |
|---|---|---|---|
| Local Sources | $455,966 | $443,500 | $354,144 |
| State Sources | 4,309,844 | 4,500,000 | 4,847,963 |
| Federal Sources | 2,023,289 | 1,750,000 | 2,343,186 |
| Total Revenues | 6,789,099 | 6,693,500 | 7,545,293 |
| Total Expenditures | 6,204,143 | 6,398,307 | 8,731,566 |
| Net Change in Fund Balance | 584,956 | 295,193 | (1,186,273) |
| Fund Balance End of Year | $3,600,167 | $3,099,136 | $2,413,894 |

Highlights: contractual obligation reconciled; projected $1.2 million use of fund balance; projected $2.4 million fund balance; $1.6 million remaining excess fund balance; $1.4 million set to be spent on Troy High Kitchen.

**Other Ancillary Fund Highlights**
Community Service Fund: projected $(278k) operating deficit, projected $1.8 million fund balance, and a reminder of no Federal Childcare Stabilization funds in FY2025. Preschool Fund: $95k projected operating surplus, $2.3 million projected fund balance, Universal Preschool as the Governor's initiative for 25-26, and no Federal Childcare Stabilization funds in FY2025. TCC Fund: revenues equal expenditures. Sinking Fund: $433k projected operating surplus and $509k projected fund balance.

Understanding school funding (2024-25). Inflation comparison. https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: A summary sheet prepared for the Oakland County School Boards Association (OCSBA) bylaws review lists each proposed 2025 revision by page, article and section with a short rationale. Four revisions are identified as clerical or grammatical and are stated not to change the meaning of the bylaws, including correcting 'off' to 'office' in Article V, Section 3 and 'Ther' to 'The' in Article VIII, Section 2. Eight further sections are revised for content, among them a new Article VII, Section 10 requiring the Board of Directors to create and maintain Board Operating Procedures, an option to split the Office of Secretary into Corresponding and Recording Secretary roles, and a shift of committee-chair elections from the first meeting after January 31st to the first meeting after July 1st. Article XVI, Section 1 would let the Board of Directors correct grammatical errors without a vote of the membership, while substantive amendments still go to Member School Districts on a written ballot with at least a forty (40) day voting period.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
Overview
OCSBA Bylaws - Amendments at a Glance is a change-log style handout accompanying the Oakland County School Boards Association's proposed 2025 bylaws revisions. Each entry gives the page number, article, section, the revised language and a rationale. The revisions are divided into two groups: four clerical/grammatical changes stated not to change the meaning of the bylaws, and eight sections revised and edited for content.

Clerical and grammatical revisions
| # | Page | Article / Section | Change and rationale |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 3 | Article V, Sec. 3 - Place of Meeting | 'off' is supposed to read 'office' (registered office of the Association) |
| 2 | 6 | Article VIII, Sec. 2 - Term of Office | Delete the stray 'r' so 'Ther' reads 'The' |
| 3 | 9 | Article IX, Sec. 4 - Government Relations Committee | Add 'on' after 'information' |
| 4 | 15 | Article XIV, Sec. 2 - Dealing with the Association | Remove a duplicated phrase |

Revisions edited for content
| # | Page | Article / Section | Substance |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 5 | Article VII, Sec. 4 - Notice | Delete references to notice by U.S. mail and fax as outdated modes of communication; special-meeting notice given at least two days by written notice delivered personally, by phone or email |
| 2 | 6 | Article VII, Sec. 10 - Board Operating Procedures | New section: the Board shall create and maintain Board Operating Procedures to be used with the Bylaws, reflecting procedures recently adopted that define roles, responsibilities and timelines |
| 3 | 7 | Article VIII, Sec. 6 - The Secretary | At the discretion of the Board on an annual basis, the Office of Secretary may be divided into Corresponding Secretary and Recording Secretary; rationale cites a Board of 7-9 directors and added leadership opportunities |
| 4 | 8 | Article IX, Sec. 3 - Committee Chairs | Chair election moves from the first committee meeting after January 31st to the first meeting after July 1st, aligning with the Operating Year of July 1 - June 30; written notice of the election at least seven (7) calendar days in advance |
| 5 | 9 | Article IX, Sec. 4 - Government Relations Committee | Standing committee meeting at least 6 times per year; each Member School District appoints a representative at its annual organizational meeting; chair elected annually at the first committee meeting after January 31st with one (1) vote per district; in the absence of an elected Vice Chair the Vice President of OCSBA assumes the position |
| 6 | 9 | Article IX, Sec. 5 - Resolutions and Bylaws Committee | Standing committee meeting at least once per year; appointments made by the OCSBA President rather than the Board of Directors; the Government Relations Committee Chairperson shall be a member |
| 7 | 16 | Article XV, Sec. 5 - Method of Giving Notices | Notice given by electronic communication to a director's or officer's last known district-provided email address instead of by mailing; OCSBA does not physically mail communications |
| 8 | 17 | Article XVI, Sec. 1 - Amendments | Bylaws altered or amended by vote of Member School Districts on a written ballot with at least a forty (40) day voting period, one vote per district; grammatical errors that do not change meaning or intent may be corrected by the Board of Directors without a membership vote |

Effect
The package modernizes notice practices, formalizes Board Operating Procedures, moves committee leadership elections into the July-June operating year, shifts committee appointments to the OCSBA President, builds a Vice Chair succession path for the Government Relations Committee, and allows routine grammatical corrections during annual review without sending the matter to the Member School Districts.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
OCSBA Bylaws - Amendments at a Glance is the change-log companion document to the Oakland County School Boards Association's proposed 2025 bylaws revisions, presented in the Troy School District Board of Education packet for the May 6, 2025 meeting. It organizes the proposed edits into two groups, giving for each the page of the bylaws, the article and section affected, the revised text, and a rationale.

Group one: clerical and grammatical revisions

The document states that the following four revisions are clerical/grammatical in nature and do not change the meaning of the bylaws.

1. Page 3, Article V, Section 3 - Place of Meeting. The Board of Directors may designate the place of meeting for any annual or regular meeting or for any special meeting. If no designation is made, or if a special meeting is otherwise called, the place of the meeting will be the registered office of the Association; but if all of the Members meet at any time and place and consent to holding of a meeting, such meeting will be valid without call or notice, and at such meeting any corporate action may be taken. Rationale: grammar and clarification - 'off' is supposed to be 'office.'

2. Page 6, Article VIII, Section 2 - Term of Office. The term of office for all officers shall commence upon their election or appointment and shall continue until the next annual meeting of the Association and thereafter until their respective successors are chosen or until their resignation or removal. Any officer may be removed from office at any meeting of the Directors, with cause, by the affirmative vote of a majority of the Directors, whenever in their judgment the best interests of the Association will be served thereby. An officer may resign by written notice to the Association; the resignation is effective upon receipt or at a subsequent time specified in the notice. The Directors have power to fill any vacancies in any offices occurring for whatever reason. Rationale: grammar/clarity - deleting the 'r' in the first word to change 'Ther' to 'The.'

3. Page 9, Article IX, Section 4 - The Government Relations Committee. The Government Relations Committee shall be a standing committee whose purpose is to receive information on legislative matters for the purpose of sharing said information with the Member School Districts to advocate for, and increase awareness of, issues facing public education. The committee will meet at least 6 times per year. Rationale: grammar/clarification, adding 'on' after 'information.'

4. Page 15, Article XIV, Section 2 - Dealing with the Association. The section addresses contracts or other transactions between the Association and one or more of its directors or officers, or between the Association and a domestic or foreign corporation, firm or association in which one or more of the Association's directors or officers are trustees or officers or are otherwise interested; such a transaction is not void or voidable solely because of such common trusteeship, officership or interest, or solely because such directors are present at the meeting of the Board of Directors or committee at which the contract or transaction is acted upon, or solely because their votes are counted, if specified conditions are satisfied. Rationale: to remove a duplicate phrase.

Group two: sections revised and edited for content

1. Page 5, Article VII, Section 4 - Notice. Notice of any special meeting of the Board of Directors will be given at least two days by written notice delivered personally, by phone, fax, or email to each Director's contact information as shown by the records of the Association, or five days' notice by mail; the mail and fax language is struck. The retained text preserves the rules that any Director may waive notice, that attendance constitutes a waiver except where a Director attends for the express purpose of objecting that the meeting was not lawfully called or convened, and that neither the business to be transacted at, nor the purpose of, any regular or special meeting need be specified in the notice or waiver unless specifically required by law or by the Bylaws. Rationale: deleting language that refers to sending meeting notices via U.S. mail and fax, which are outdated modes of communication.

2. Page 6, Article VII, Section 10 - Board Operating Procedures. A new section providing that the Board of Directors shall create and maintain Board Operating Procedures which shall be used in conjunction with these Bylaws. Rationale: the Board of Directors recently adopted Board Operating Procedures that further define roles, responsibilities and timelines.

3. Page 7, Article VIII, Section 6 - The Secretary. The Secretary shall attend all meetings of the Board of Directors and record all votes and the minutes of all proceedings in a book kept for that purpose; shall give, or cause to be given, notice of all meetings of the Directors for which notice may be required; shall perform other duties as prescribed by the Directors; and shall have authority to execute with the President all authorized conveyances, contracts or other obligations in the name of the Association, except as otherwise directed by the Directors. Added language provides that, at the discretion of the Board of Directors on an annual basis, the Office of Secretary may be divided into two roles: Corresponding Secretary and Recording Secretary. Rationale: with a Board of 7-9 directors it is helpful to split the role of Secretary into two, and it provides additional leadership opportunities.

4. Page 8, Article IX, Section 3 - Committee Chairs. Each standing and ad hoc committee shall elect a Chairperson annually from the appointed representatives. The election shall be the first order of business at the committee's first meeting after July 1st, replacing January 31st, unless otherwise specified in the Bylaws. Written notice of the election date, time and place shall be provided to all appointed representatives not less than seven (7) calendar days prior to the meeting at which the vote will occur. Rationale: the Operating Year is July 1 - June 30, and this change will bring the Association into alignment.

5. Page 9, Article IX, Section 4 - The Government Relations Committee. Beyond the grammatical fix noted above, added Committee Membership/Leadership language provides that at each Member School District's annual organizational meeting a Member should be appointed to represent that district on the Government Relations Committee; that a Committee Chairperson will be elected annually from the appointed Members at the first committee meeting after January 31st; that each Member School District in attendance shall have one (1) vote, cast by the district's appointed representative; and that in the absence of an elected Vice Chair, the Vice President of OCSBA will assume the position of Vice Chair. Rationale: to ensure the Association is building leadership on the GRC.

6. Page 9, Article IX, Section 5 - Resolutions and Bylaws Committee. The committee shall be a standing committee exercising the powers prescribed in the section, with the purpose of developing and managing the resolutions and bylaws process, and shall meet at least once per year. Under Committee Membership/Leadership, committee members will be appointed annually by the OCSBA President rather than by the Board of Directors, may be reappointed for additional terms, and will elect a Committee Chairperson at the first committee meeting after appointment. The Government Relations Committee Chairperson shall be a member of the Resolutions and Bylaws Committee. Rationale: common practice is that the OCSBA President makes committee appointments.

7. Page 16, Article XV, Section 5 - Method of Giving Notices. Any notice required by statute or by the Bylaws to be given to the directors, or to any officers of the Association unless otherwise provided in the Bylaws or in any statute, shall be given by electronic communication, replacing mailing, to such director or officer at his or her last known district-provided email address as the same appears on the records of the Association, and such notice shall be deemed to have been given at the time of such communication. Rationale: OCSBA does not physically mail communications.

8. Page 17, Article XVI, Section 1 - Amendments. The Bylaws may be altered or amended by the vote of the Member School Districts. The Board of Directors will provide a written ballot with the proposed amendment(s) to each Member School District, giving at least a forty (40) day period in which to vote, and each Member School District will have one vote. New language provides that grammatical errors that do not change the meaning or intent of the language may be corrected by the Board of Directors without a vote of the membership. Rationale: small grammatical errors such as grammar and spelling that do not change meaning or intent can be corrected by the Board of Directors during the annual review rather than having to go out to membership for a vote.

Taken together, the at-a-glance sheet documents a package that modernizes notice practices by removing mail and fax, codifies Board Operating Procedures, permits an annual split of the Secretary's office, realigns committee chair elections with the July 1 - June 30 operating year, moves committee appointments to the OCSBA President, creates a Vice Chair succession path for the Government Relations Committee through the OCSBA Vice President, converts official notices to district-provided email, and gives the Board authority to fix non-substantive grammatical errors without a membership ballot.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: The full Bylaws of the Oakland County School Boards Association are presented in redline form, showing the 2025 proposed edits in context alongside their rationales. The document records adoption by the Board of Directors on 11/15/2017, adoption by the General Membership on 1/24/2018 and 10/18/2018, and amendments approved by Member School Districts on 9/16/2020, 9/10/2021 and 3/3/2023, and locates the Association's principal office at 2111 Pontiac Lake Road, Waterford Township, County of Oakland. Sixteen articles cover offices, purpose, membership, dues, meetings, election of a Board of no fewer than 7 nor more than 9 directors serving three-year terms, officers, committees, dissolution, fiduciary and financial responsibilities, indemnification, fiscal year, conflicts, miscellaneous provisions and amendments, followed by an Appendix 1 definition of cause for removal adopted September 16, 2020. Expenditures exceeding $2,500 require Board of Directors approval and the signatures of both the President and the Treasurer.

Identification and adoption history
Bylaws of the Oakland County School Boards Association, shown with proposed changes and rationales. Adopted by Board of Directors 11/15/2017; adopted by General Membership 1/24/2018 and 10/18/2018; amendments approved by Member School Districts 9/16/2020, 9/10/2021 and 3/3/2023. Principal office: 2111 Pontiac Lake Road, Waterford Township, County of Oakland, Michigan.

Membership, dues and member meetings (Articles III-V)
Membership is open to any publicly elected board of education member of a school district located in Oakland County, or any elected Oakland ISD Board of Education member, whose district is also in good standing with the Michigan Association of School Boards. Each Member has one vote, with Member School Districts casting one vote each on resolutions and bylaws amendments. Electronic voting is granted to the Board of Directors only for emergency business, reaffirmed at the next Board meeting. Financing comes from an annual MASB grant to its County Area School Boards Association (CASBA) members, Intermediate School District dues not to exceed the MASB CASBA grant, and contributions and gifts. There is an annual meeting plus not less than three additional regular membership meetings each year, the annual meeting being the first regular meeting after July 1. Special meetings require 30 days' notice; written notice of member meetings is delivered personally or by email not less than ten nor more than fifty days before the meeting. Quorum is at least one Member from twenty-five (25%) percent of the Member School Districts.

Board of Directors and officers (Articles VI-VIII)
| Provision | Requirement |
| --- | --- |
| Number of directors | Odd number, no fewer than 7 nor more than 9 |
| Term | Three (3) years |
| Election Committee | Convened by May 1 yearly, three most recently elected Board members |
| Election | June meeting; written ballot if candidates exceed vacancies |
| Attendance | Three (3) consecutive missed meetings constitutes resignation; excused-absence request in writing within thirty (30) days |
| Special meeting notice | At least two days written notice (mail/fax language struck) |
| Officers | President, Vice-President, Secretary, Treasurer elected from the current Board |
| New Sec. 10 | Board shall create and maintain Board Operating Procedures |
| Secretary | May be divided annually into Corresponding Secretary and Recording Secretary |

Committees (Article IX)
Committee quorum is twenty-five (25%) percent of appointed representatives, one vote each. Chairs are elected annually, the election being the first order of business at the first committee meeting after July 1st (changed from January 31st), with at least seven (7) calendar days' written notice. The Government Relations Committee is a standing committee meeting at least 6 times per year; the Vice President of OCSBA assumes the Vice Chair position if none is elected. The Resolutions and Bylaws Committee meets at least once per year, with members appointed by the OCSBA President. Member School District voting windows on resolutions and bylaws amendments run at least forty (40) calendar days, and resolutions approved by at least nineteen (19) Member School Districts become the official position of the Association.

Financial and legal provisions (Articles X-XVI, Appendix 1)
Expenditures may not exceed the approved annual budget; those exceeding $2,500 require Board approval plus signatures of the President and Treasurer, while expenditures up to $2,500 may be approved by either the President or the Treasurer, and the Vice-President may approve if they are absent or disabled. Reports are distributed quarterly; the Treasurer presents a budget for the upcoming fiscal year (July 1 to June 30) no later than the June Board meeting and end-of-year revenue and expense reports no later than August 30. An external audit is conducted only if required by law or a third party. The Board may enter an Administrative and Financial Services Agreement with Oakland Schools. No earnings may inure to any Member, Director or Officer, as prohibited by Section 501(c)(4) of the Internal Revenue Code of 1986. Indemnification follows the Michigan Nonprofit Association Act. Notices to directors and officers move to electronic communication at district-provided email addresses. Bylaws are amended by Member School District ballot with at least a forty (40) day voting period. Appendix 1, adopted by the OCSBA Board of Directors on September 16, 2020, defines cause for removal by reference to the duties of care, loyalty and obedience.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
The Bylaws of the Oakland County School Boards Association are reproduced in full with the 2025 proposed changes shown in place and each change followed by its rationale. The cover block records: Adopted by Board of Directors 11/15/2017; Adopted by General Membership 1/24/2018 and 10/18/2018; Amendments Approved by Member School Districts 9/16/2020, 9/10/2021 and 3/3/2023.

Article I - Offices. The principal office of the Association in the State of Michigan is located at 2111 Pontiac Lake Road, Waterford Township, County of Oakland. The Association may have other offices within or without Michigan as the Board of Directors determines. It must continuously maintain a registered office and a registered agent whose office is identical with the registered office; the registered office need not be identical with the principal office and its address may be changed by the Board.

Article II - Purpose. The eight stated purposes are: (a) to advance the quality of public education in Oakland County through the cooperative efforts of locally elected boards of education; (b) to promote high standards in educational programs and services; (c) to make information on educational issues available to school board members; (d) to conduct and sponsor meetings and programs in partnership with Oakland Schools; (e) to promote public understanding of the role of school boards and the need for citizen involvement; (f) to enhance cooperation and communication among boards of education in Oakland County; (g) to present a strong force representing the views of Oakland County school boards to political representatives; and (h) to advocate for county, state and national legislation and governance supporting public education services by locally elected boards.

Article III - Membership. Any publicly elected Board of Education member of a school district located in Oakland County, or any elected Oakland ISD Board of Education member (collectively 'Member School Districts'), whose district is also a member in good standing of the Michigan Association of School Boards (MASB), is an eligible general Member. Each Member is entitled to one vote, exercised in person, with the exception that each Member School District has one (1) vote on resolutions under Article IX and on bylaws amendments under Article XVI; district votes are recorded on receipt of the completed resolution or ballot indicating the vote of the district's Trustees and must be received before the stated deadline, with results provided to all Member Districts not later than the next general membership meeting. Electronic voting rights are granted to the Board of Directors only for emergency business, with all electronic votes reaffirmed at the next Board meeting. Membership is not transferable or assignable.

Article IV - Dues. The Association is financed by an annual MASB grant to its County Area School Boards Association (CASBA) members, by Intermediate School District membership dues in an amount not to exceed the MASB CASBA grant, and by contributions and gifts accepted by the Association.

Article V - Meetings of Members. There shall be an annual meeting and not less than three additional regular membership meetings each year for appointing the Board of Directors and other business; the annual meeting is the first regular meeting after July 1. Special meetings may be called by voice or email by the President or by two or more members of the Board of Directors with 30 days' notice. Section 3 fixes the place of meeting as the registered office if no designation is made, with the 'off'/'office' correction noted. Written notice of member meetings stating place, day and hour is delivered personally or by email by the Secretary not less than ten nor more than fifty days before the meeting. Members may act without a meeting by written consent signed by all Members entitled to vote. Quorum is the presence of at least one Member from twenty-five (25%) percent of the Member School Districts. Superintendents and administrators of Member School Districts are encouraged to participate.

Article VI - Election of Board of Directors. The Board consists of an odd number of Directors, no fewer than 7 nor more than 9, with the Board having discretion to set the number; a change must be considered whenever an election produces fewer candidates than open seats and before seeking candidates to fill a vacancy. A decrease is accomplished by attrition, which may result in an eight member Board for up to one year until the next election; an increase is accomplished by election, and the Board may call a mid-year special election to increase the number. Only one Member from each Member School District may serve at any given time. The term of office is three (3) years and continues until a successor is elected and qualified. By May 1st yearly the Board convenes an Election Committee comprised of the three most recently elected Members of the Board, which seeks candidates creating a Board with geographical balance throughout Oakland County; Board Candidate Application Forms are sent to all Member School Districts, nominations cannot be made from the floor, and the election takes place at the June meeting, by written ballot if there are more candidates than vacancies. Directors may resign by written notice and may be removed by the Members or the Board with cause as defined in Appendix I by affirmative vote of a majority of the Members or the Directors then in office, excluding the Director who is the subject of the action. On a vacancy, the Board first considers decreasing the number of Directors; otherwise the President notifies Members, application forms are sent to each district, and the Board appoints a member at its next meeting to serve until the next scheduled election. Failure to attend three (3) consecutive Board meetings constitutes a resignation, though the Board may grant an excused absence on written request to the Board President within thirty (30) days of the missed meeting.

Article VII - Board of Directors. The Board carries out the purposes specified in Article II of the Articles of Incorporation. A regular annual meeting is held without other notice than the Bylaws, with date and time set by the Board. Special meetings may be called by the President or any two Directors. Section 4 provides notice of special meetings at least two days by written notice delivered personally, by phone, fax, or email, or five days' notice by mail, with the mail and fax language struck; the rationale states that U.S. mail and fax are outdated modes of communication. Attendance waives notice except where a Director attends expressly to object that the meeting was not lawfully called or convened. A majority of the Board constitutes a quorum, and the act of a majority of the Directors serving, whether elected or appointed, at a meeting at which a quorum is present is the act of the Board. Directors receive no stated salaries, though a fixed sum and expenses of attendance may be allowed by resolution. Action may be taken without a meeting by written consent signed by all Directors. Records and business of Board proceedings are confidential absent advance authorization. New Section 10 requires the Board to create and maintain Board Operating Procedures used in conjunction with the Bylaws, the rationale citing recently adopted procedures defining roles, responsibilities and timelines.

Article VIII - Officers. As soon as practical after the annual appointment of Directors, the Board elects from the current Board a President, Vice-President, Secretary and Treasurer. Section 2 corrects 'Ther' to 'The' and provides that terms commence upon election or appointment and continue until the next annual meeting and thereafter until successors are chosen or upon resignation or removal; an officer may be removed with cause by affirmative vote of a majority of the Directors. Officers receive no stated salaries. The President is Chief Executive Officer with general and active management of activities and presides at all meetings of the Directors. The Vice-President performs the President's duties in the President's absence or disability; if both are absent the Directors present designate another presiding officer. The Secretary attends all Board meetings, records all votes and minutes in a book kept for that purpose, gives notice of meetings, and may execute with the President all authorized conveyances, contracts or other obligations; added language allows the Board, at its discretion on an annual basis, to divide the Office of Secretary into Corresponding Secretary and Recording Secretary, the rationale citing a Board of 7-9 directors and additional leadership opportunities. The Treasurer has custody of funds and securities, keeps full and accurate accounts of receipts and disbursements, deposits monies in designated depositories, disburses funds as ordered by the Directors, reports on transactions and financial condition, and if required gives the Association a bond. Under Section 8, all officers must furnish bonds if the Board requires, with the Association assuming the cost.

Article IX - Committees. The Board may designate standing and ad hoc committees. Unless otherwise stated, the presence of twenty-five (25%) percent of appointed representatives constitutes a quorum and each appointed representative present has one vote; districts may designate alternates, counted for quorum or vote only when the primary representative is absent. Section 3 provides that each standing and ad hoc committee elects a Chairperson annually from the appointed representatives, the election being the first order of business at the committee's first meeting after July 1st (changed from January 31st) with written notice of the election date, time and place not less than seven (7) calendar days prior; the rationale is that the Operating Year is July 1 - June 30. Chairs establish and distribute meeting schedules and agendas, maintain attendance records, distribute minutes, and report to the Board through the President; a Chair may resign by written notice to the President or be removed without cause by majority vote of appointed representatives present or of the Board then in office. Section 4 makes the Government Relations Committee a standing committee meeting at least 6 times per year, with the 'information on' grammatical fix; each Member School District should appoint a representative at its annual organizational meeting, a Chairperson is elected annually at the first committee meeting after January 31st with one (1) vote per district cast by its appointed representative, and in the absence of an elected Vice Chair the Vice President of OCSBA assumes the position. The committee reviews and revises Legislative Priorities annually, submits them to the Board for approval, and once approved they go to the Resolutions and Bylaws Committee and Member School Districts. Section 5 makes the Resolutions and Bylaws Committee a standing committee meeting at least once per year, with members appointed annually by the OCSBA President rather than the Board of Directors, eligible for reappointment, electing a Chairperson at the first meeting after appointment; the Government Relations Committee Chairperson shall be a member. Resolutions or bylaws revisions may be initiated by a Member School District Board, the Board of Directors, the Government Relations Committee or the Resolutions and Bylaws Committee, must be submitted in writing, and are addressed at the committee's next meeting. The Board reviews all proposals before submission to Member School Districts, which are asked to vote at their next meeting; the voting window is at least forty (40) calendar days with the deadline specified on the ballot or resolution. Resolutions approved by at least nineteen (19) Member School Districts become the official position of the Association as interpreted and pursued by its Board of Directors.

Article X - Dissolution. On dissolution, all assets are distributed as provided in Article VIII of the Articles of Incorporation. No part of net earnings may be distributed to or inure to the benefit of any Member, Director or Officer, as prohibited by Section 501(c)(4) of the Internal Revenue Code of 1986, as amended, or the Michigan General Sales Tax Act or the Michigan Use Tax Act.

Article XI - Fiduciary and Financial Responsibilities. Expenditures may not exceed the approved annual budget, and no committee may create financial liability unless specifically authorized by a majority of the Members. Board of Directors approval and signatures of both the President and Treasurer are required for any expenditure exceeding $2,500; expenditures up to $2,500 must be approved by either the Board President or the Treasurer, and the Vice-President may approve if the President and/or Treasurer are absent or disabled. Reports are completed timely and distributed to all Board members quarterly or on request. The Treasurer presents for Board approval a budget for the upcoming fiscal year (July 1 to June 30) not later than the June Board of Directors meeting, and end-of-year revenue and expense reports for the immediately preceding fiscal year no later than August 30th. The approved budget and annual report of income and expenditures are presented at the first fall Member Meeting, and accounting records are closed annually in preparation for IRS filings. Annually the Association performs agreed upon procedures on its financial records, with the year-end report available to the Board before the annual Board and Member meetings; an external audit is conducted in place of the agreed upon procedures only if required by law or a third party. The Board may enter an Administrative and Financial Services Agreement with Oakland Schools to support management of the Association, with the Treasurer monitoring the work performed.

Article XII - Indemnification of Officers, Directors, Employees and Agents. Eleven sections provide indemnification to the fullest extent authorized by the Michigan Nonprofit Association Act for third-party claims and for claims brought by or in the right of the Association, covering expenses including attorneys' fees, judgments, penalties, fines and settlement amounts where the Indemnitee acted in good faith. Indemnification is not available for actions brought by the Indemnitee unless authorized by the Board or brought to enforce the Article and successful. Approval is determined by majority vote of a quorum of Directors not parties to the action, or if unobtainable by a committee of not less than two (2) disinterested Directors, or by independent legal counsel in a written opinion. Expenses are advanced upon an unlimited general obligation undertaking to repay. Partial indemnification, indemnification of employees and agents, non-exclusivity of rights with a cap at actual expenses incurred, continuation for former directors and officers and their heirs, executors and administrators, power to purchase liability insurance, severability, and definitions of 'other enterprises,' 'fines' and 'serving at the request of the Association' complete the Article.

Articles XIII-XVI and Appendix 1. The fiscal year is determined by the Board of Directors. Article XIV requires officers, directors, committee members and employees to avoid conflicts; Section 2, with a duplicate phrase removed, addresses transactions with interested directors or officers, which are not void or voidable solely because of common trusteeship, officership or interest if the transaction is fair and reasonable when authorized, approved or ratified, or if material facts are disclosed and the transaction is approved by a vote sufficient without counting the interested director. Interested persons must give notice and refrain from voting or exerting influence, are not counted toward quorum on the matter, and the minutes must reflect the disclosure, the abstention and the quorum situation. Article XV covers contracts and conveyances, execution of instruments, borrowing, adjourned meetings, and Section 5 Method of Giving Notices, revised so notices to directors and officers are given by electronic communication to the last known district-provided email address, deemed given at the time of communication, because OCSBA does not physically mail communications. It also permits action by written consent filed with the minutes, remote participation by conference telephone or similar two-way communication equipment counting as presence in person by oral or written permission of a majority of the Board, and describes a corporate seal inscribed with the Association's name and the words 'Corporate Seal' and 'Michigan.' Article XVI provides that the Bylaws may be altered or amended by vote of the Member School Districts on a written ballot with at least a forty (40) day voting period, one vote per district, with new language allowing the Board to correct grammatical errors that do not change meaning or intent without a membership vote; the Board may adopt additional rules and regulations not inconsistent with the Articles of Incorporation or Bylaws unless a local, state or national emergency has been declared, and during a declared emergency may set aside rules and regulations regarding meetings, elections and the conduct of Association affairs. Appendix 1, Definition of Cause for Removing a Board Member or Officer, adopted by the OCSBA Board of Directors on September 16, 2020, recites the nonprofit duties of care, loyalty and obedience and defines cause as acts of malfeasance, misfeasance or nonfeasance; willful failure to follow OCSBA bylaws; willful neglect of duties; failure to disclose a conflict of interest or using the Association for personal gain; using the Board position or OCSBA's logo in a political endorsement; frequently missed Board or committee meetings; creating an unhealthy or dysfunctional boardroom through inappropriate behavior or disrespect; and ethical concerns such as discrimination, harassment or criminal behaviors.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
OCSBA Resolutions Showing Changes sets out the Oakland County School Boards Association's legislative resolutions in redline, distinguishing 2025 recommended amendments to previously adopted resolutions from continuing resolutions. An introductory note states that the resolutions have been adopted by member school districts and that adoption and/or amendment dates are noted for each. It quotes OCSBA Bylaws Article IX, Section 5, Resolution Adoption: resolutions that are approved by at least nineteen (19) member school districts shall be the official position of the association as interpreted and pursued by its board of directors. Page footers read 'Revised March, 2023.'

2025 recommended amendments to previously adopted resolutions

Accountability and Transparency [OCSBA Adopted 9/24/2019]. OCSBA supports transparency and accountability for ALL school aid funds - naming community governed public school districts, charter schools, cyber schools, community colleges and public universities - holding every school that receives public funding to the same accountability and transparency standards, including FOIA requests and the Open Meetings Act. The scope expressly includes local districts, ISDs, Public School Academies (also known as charter schools), their authorizers and management companies, as well as all colleges and universities. Cited authority: MASB Resolution A 6.65 (c), (d), (f). Rationale: expanded to include FOIA requests, OMA and additional school entities.

Broadband Access and Devices [OCSBA Adopted 9/11/2021]. The resolution states that broadband should be included in any federal or state infrastructure plan; that OCSBA supports additional federal and state funding opportunities to expand affordable and reliable broadband access; that OCSBA supports federal and state programs for the purchase of internet capable devices and software; and adds that OCSBA supports dedicated resources for cybersecurity. Cited authority: MASB Resolution A-10.30 - 2021 amendment. Rationale: (a) update 'we support' to 'OCSBA supports' in all resolutions; (b) cybersecurity is a growing issue and needs dedicated funding and support.

Mental Health [OCSBA Adopted 9/24/2019]. OCSBA supports increased mental health services and professionals in schools and adequate state resources providing, at a minimum, annual inflation adjusted state resources to allow schools to both educate and keep students and staff safe. Sub-bullets call for helping staff identify potential mental health issues for students and encouraging the Michigan Department of Education (MDE) to develop a model policy for staff regarding identifying mental health issues and appropriate staff response. Cited authority: MASB Resolutions G 9.01; G 9.05; G 9.50. Rationale: districts need consistent, annual funding for mental health.

School Aid [OCSBA Adopted 9/24/2019]. The redline shows a struck bullet A opposing the use of School Aid Fund dollars for any purpose other than K-12 education [MASB Resolution A 10.25], replaced by a new first bullet specifying that the School Aid Fund is only for Pre-K to 12th grade public education in Michigan's Constitution and opposing any attempts to create private school vouchers or tax credit programs [MASB Resolutions A 10.25 (a) and A 10.05]. Bullet B supports additional funding for Special Education, At-Risk and ELL students [MASB Resolutions A 10.25 (g) and (j); A 10.55]. Bullet C protects the School Aid Fund and local revenues from state tax policy changes [MASB Resolutions A 10.25 (c); A 10.55]. The former bullet D containing the same constitutional/voucher language is struck, and the surviving bullet D provides that OCSBA supports enacting the annual School Aid Budget no later than June 1 so that school districts have factual information to meet their constitutional and statutory requirement to approve a budget by June 30 [MASB Resolution A 10.25 (h)]. Rationale: A and D were duplicative, so D moves to the first bullet.

School Finance Research Collaborative (SFRC) [OCSBA Adopted 9/24/2019; Amended 9/11/2021; 3/3/2023]. OCSBA supports implementation of the recommendations of the SFRC, with the trailing clause limiting that support to the recommended additional studies on capital costs, infrastructure and transportation shown struck. The resolution retains the requirement that while implementing the SFRC recommendations, higher funded districts must be held harmless. Cited authority: MASB resolution G 11.01 and A-10.25 - 2021 amendment. Rationale: those recommended studies have been completed, so the association now supports all of the SFRC's recommendations.

School Nutrition [OCSBA Adopted 3/3/2023]. OCSBA supports the expansion of the Free and Reduced Meals program to include all children, with the phrase 'as was done during the pandemic' shown struck in favor of 'codification of free universal meals.'

Teacher Shortages [OCSBA Adopted 9/11/2021]. OCSBA supports statewide initiatives to address teacher shortages and retain teachers while maintaining quality teacher preparation programs. Initiatives might include, but should not be limited to, incentives to enter and complete a teaching college program, incentives for teachers to remain in the classroom, and easing the process to obtain Michigan certification for teachers certified in other states. Cited authority: MASB 2021-2022 Legislative Priority. Rationale: replace 'we' with OCSBA to be consistent across resolutions.

Universal Preschool / Early Childhood [OCSBA Adopted 9/24/2019]. The heading 'Universal Preschool' is struck in favor of 'Early Childhood.' OCSBA supports additional new dollars to fund universal, public preschool for all four year old children, and adds that OCSBA supports mandatory kindergarten for all five-year-old children [OCSBA Adopted 9/24/2019; MASB Resolution A 6.15 (c)]. Rationale: (a) public preschool dollars should not be used for vouchers or private or parochial preschools; (b) add support for mandatory kindergarten, since kindergarten is not currently mandatory in the State of Michigan.

When Aligned With OCSBA Legislative Priorities, OCSBA Also Supports [OCSBA Adopted 9/24/2019]. The listed agendas are the National School Boards Association (NSBA) Legislative Agenda, the Michigan Association of School Boards (MASB) Legislative Agenda, the Oakland County Superintendents Association (OCSA) Legislative Agenda, and the newly added Consortium of State School Board Associations (COSSBA) Legislative Agenda. Rationale: adding COSSBA to the list of associations with whom OCSBA aligns, since MASB belongs to both NSBA and COSSBA. Reference links are provided for MASB Resolutions (https://www.masb.org/resolutions.aspx), NSBA Advocacy: IDEA (https://www.nsba.org/Advocacy), and COSSBA Advocacy (https://www.cossba.org/advocacy).

Continuing resolutions previously adopted by members

Evidence-Based Decision Making [OCSBA Adopted 9/24/2019]: OCSBA supports evidence-based education policy that will maximize opportunities for the highest achievement of each student [MASB Resolution G 11.01].

Lame Duck [OCSBA Adopted 9/24/2019]: OCSBA supports lame duck parameters that will address introduction and accelerated passage of legislation after the November election.

Local Control [OCSBA Adopted 9/24/2019]: support local control of community-governed public schools with elected school boards [MASB Resolution A 10.10; A 10.55; A 12.70]. The continuing-resolution section also carries forward the mental health sub-bullets on helping staff identify potential mental health issues for students and encouraging MDE to develop a model policy for staff regarding identifying mental health issues and appropriate staff response.

School Safety [OCSBA Adopted 3/3/2023]: OCSBA supports that there be adequate state resources to allow schools to both educate and keep students and staff safe.

Special Education [OCSBA Adopted 9/24/2019]: OCSBA supports full funding of the federal Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA), noting that although federal legislation initially promised to provide 40 percent of the excess cost to educate students with disabilities, the appropriations have fallen short, leaving states and local school districts to make up the difference [MASB Resolution A 5.01; NSBA Advocacy: IDEA].

Unfunded Mandates [OCSBA Adopted 9/24/2019]: OCSBA opposes any state or federal legislation that results in increased costs for school districts without full funding, and also encourages the Michigan Legislature to oppose any federal laws or programs that are not fully funded and thus cost the state valuable resources [MASB Resolution A 10.20].

The overall effect of the 2025 package is to broaden accountability language to reach charter authorizers, management companies and higher education under FOIA and the Open Meetings Act; to add cybersecurity funding and mandatory kindergarten as new positions; to remove duplicative School Aid language while retaining the June 1 budget-enactment position; to convert conditional SFRC support into support for the full set of recommendations; to codify universal free school meals; to align the association with COSSBA in addition to NSBA, MASB and OCSA; and to standardize the voice of every resolution on 'OCSBA supports.'

Results: 13 kindergarten students plan to attend; 1 first grade student plans to attend; 17 middle school students plan to attend across grades 6-8, comprising 14 sixth graders, 2 seventh graders and 1 eighth grader.

**Memorandum text and residual prior-year language**
The memo lists the factors considered: current enrollment across the Troy School District; enrollment projections, patterns and trends; numbers and percentages of Schools of Choice students currently in the district; the projected number of Schools of Choice siblings who would be age-eligible to enter the district if a "Limited" number of kindergarten, first and sixth through eighth grade students were admitted; and available elementary classrooms. The document also carries an older, unedited passage written for the 2016-2017 school year. That passage recommends using Fred Ignatovich's 1.5 enrollment projection numbers with his recommended formula (most likely plus low divided by 2); notes that in "Document 1" the actual February Count enrollment for both kindergarten and first grade was above Ignatovich's "Most Likely" and "Low" 2015-16 projections; recommends accepting SOC applications for 100 kindergarten and 30 first grade students with the expectation of more than 100 kindergarten applicants and the option to admit additional students in the third week of August; limits SOC kindergarten applicants to the full-day kindergarten program; and accepts "Sibling Preference" applications only for siblings of current SOC students to attend Baker Middle School, where enrollment next year was estimated to approximate 728 and accepting 15 applications in the initial process would bring the building close to an ideal total student population.

**2023-2024 recommendations**
After analyzing the data, the administration recommends that the district use Plante Moran Cresa enrollment projection numbers as the foundation for determining the number of Schools of Choice students to admit for 2023-2024; accept SOC applications for 13 kindergarten, 1 first grade and 17 middle school students; admit 13 kindergartners initially with the option of admitting additional students in the third week of August if space allows, noting the district anticipates attracting many more than 13 applicants; and place middle school students in a building according to available space.

**Report**
"Elementary Mathematics Materials Adoption," March 2023, submitted by Natalie Haezebrouck and Julia Alder to the Troy School District Board of Education (March 7, 2023 meeting).

**Rationale**
The district reviews curricular materials every nine years. The last curricular adoption was Middle and High-School Health in 2020; the last elementary math adoption was conducted in 2010. The review philosophy has shifted from simply seeking new materials to a comprehensive program review covering instructional practices, intervention, assessment and current data, so that curricular, structural and staffing needs can be aligned. Teachers have been supplementing the current resource with three act tasks, number sense routines and additional materials; a resource that fully addresses deep conceptual learning, number sense and mathematical fluency is desired.

**Process**
The Math Leadership Team (MLT), an interdepartmental team with representation from all grade levels and roles, was assembled in September 2019. MLT reviewed student performance data, surveyed all elementary teachers, and studied the NCTM publication Principles to Action, concluding that both a math specialist role and new curricular materials were needed. MLT members and colleagues from the Oakland County Math Leadership Team identified candidate publishers and resources, screened against the Standards for Mathematical Practice, the NCTM 8 Effective Math Teaching Practices, and the Michigan Standards for Mathematics. In January 2021 the list was narrowed and select publishers were invited to Troy to demonstrate online features; materials were piloted in January and February. Ninety-five early adopter teachers volunteered to implement Bridges in Mathematics and Number Corner during the 2022-23 school year.

**Early adopter team by grade**
Kindergarten 13, grade 1 22, grade 2 13, grade 3 15, grade 4 16, grade 5 16; total 95. Building totals: Barnard 6, Bemis 6, Costello 9, Hamilton 18, Hill 6, Leonard 17, Martell 12, Morse 6, Troy Union 9, Wass 4, Wattles 2.

**Materials reviewed**
Illustrative Mathematics (not fully available during the 2021-2022 pilot window, delivered through Google Drive, hands-on materials not integrated, now more available from Kendall Hunt); Math Expressions 2013 Edition, the current resource (limited approach to fluency, did not adequately address differentiation, ELD and students with special needs); and Bridges Mathematics including Number Corner, which integrates Math Recovery learning progressions and a Fluency Pathway in Number Corner.

**Recommendation and implementation**
Bridges Math and Number Corner 3rd edition are recommended. All resources will be available on the first day of school for 2023-24. Optional training on Number Corner and Bridges Unit 1 is offered in June; all teachers participate in a kick-off during back-to-school professional development in August 2023 as part of the OneTroy kick-off, followed by job-embedded PD and math specialist support in each building.
